item.title: A boundary integral equation solver for capsule suspensions
item.description: arXiv:2611.26795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deformable capsules serve as models for biological cells, such as red blood cells, as well as for synthetic capsules in biomedical and industrial applications. In this work, we introduce a framework for fast and robust simulation of deformable capsules in three-dimensional Stokes flow, both in unbounded domains and in pipe-confined geometries. We solve the Stokes equations using a boundary integral formulation, employing a partition-of-unity discretization for the capsule membrane and the trapezoidal rule with regularization to handle the singular quadrature. Dense periodic interactions are evaluated via a fast Ewald summation scheme, achieving $O(N \log N)$ complexity for $N$ grid points. The interfacial forces on the capsule membrane are modeled using the Skalak constitutive law. We carry out a spectral analysis of this model for small perturbations of a spherical capsule, which indicates that the relaxation dynamics are intrinsically stable. However, the nonlinear character of the Skalak model induces aliasing errors that can compromise numerical stability. To address this when needed, we perform de-aliasing through upsampling and spectral filtering, and we derive guidelines for choosing appropriate filter parameters, thereby stabilizing the method. We investigate the stability and convergence behavior of the resulting scheme and conduct simulations of long-time dynamics, focusing on the relaxation of unconfined capsules and the lateral migration of pipe-confined capsules under various flow conditions.
item.dc:creator: Joar Bagge, Ziyu Du, George Biros

item.title: Droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction via pulsed electrohydrodynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.26979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical simulations based on the phase-field lattice Boltzmann method are employed to investigate droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction microchannel under pulsed electrohydrodynamics. The applied electric field modulates the interfacial morphology, thereby altering the hydrodynamic stress distribution acting on the liquid-liquid interface. Three configurations are examined: no electric field, top-biased electrode, and bottom-biased electrode. The results show that the top-biased electrode promotes rapid transverse migration of the dispersed phase towards the upper wall, thereby accelerating the transition to the channel-blocking stage. By contrast, under the bottom-biased electrode, the dispersed phase first adheres to the lower wall and subsequently deforms upward under the electric force. As a result, the droplet formation dynamics are strongly affected by the spatial distribution of the electric field. The droplet generation process is further divided into a filling stage and a squeezing stage based on theoretical analysis. During the filling stage, the electric force modifies the filling duration but has little influence on the filling flux. During the squeezing stage, the necking rate and breakup time are governed by the pinning of the dispersed-phase contact line on the channel wall. Compared with constant electric forcing, pulsed electric forcing introduces an additional temporal degree of freedom, enabling stage-dependent modulation of interfacial evolution and breakup dynamics. Finally, droplet sequence diagrams and regime maps are presented for different pulse parameters. The results demonstrate that pulsed electrohydrodynamics in a T-junction enables active and programmable control of consecutive droplet generation.
item.dc:creator: He Yan, Kang luo, Bin Gong, Lei Wang

item.title: Shear thinning confines the wall forcing: laminar chaotic mixing of Carreau fluids in a rotating arc-wall mixer
item.description: arXiv:2611.27150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With two-dimensional simulations of Carreau fluids of power-law index $N$ from 1 to 0.4, I study how shear thinning modifies laminar chaotic mixing in an open channel stirred by three arc-shaped wall segments rotating back and forth periodically, the upper one in anti-phase with the two lower ones. The outlet mixing efficiency falls monotonically, by 14 percent from $N=1$ to 0.4, mostly between $N=0.85$ and 0.6. The bulk flow and its chaotic saddle are nearly unaffected. Shear thinning acts instead through a thin layer of reduced viscosity around the moving arcs: the geometric penetration length of the wall forcing shortens as the 0.3 power of the time-mean wall viscosity, within 4 percent over a fourfold range of forcing. This confinement weakens the stretching, and the penetration length predicts the mixing efficiency ($r^2=0.97$). The optimal Strouhal number stays close to 0.7 for all fluids, but shear thinning narrows the range of efficient periods. A lamellar model indicates that the relative penalty of shear thinning grows with the Peclet number. As the injected power scales with the wall viscosity, the mixing efficiency per unit energy rises 2.6-fold from $N=1$ to 0.4, and at equal energy per unit volume, with a faster rotation, the fluid with $N=0.4$ mixes as well as the Newtonian one, and better at larger energies. In wall-driven mixers, the reach of the forcing, not the bulk viscosity, is the quantity to control.
item.dc:creator: Teodor Burghelea

item.title: Hamiltonian symmetry behind the vanishing of four-wave interactions at non-trivial resonances for one-dimensional deep-water waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.27279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The unexpected cancellation of non-trivial resonant four-wave interactions is the foundation of several compact and accurate models for one-dimensional deep-water waves. The reasons for this cancellation are not yet fully understood. An additional integral of motion would account for it, but to our knowledge no corresponding symmetry has been identified. Here it is shown that in real canonical variables with the cubic terms eliminated, the fourth-order Hamiltonian is invariant under a sign-dependent phase rotation generated by the Hilbert transform. The corresponding Noether charge is the action imbalance between right- and left-moving waves, conserved exactly although number-changing quartic terms remain. The symmetry confines the quartic kernel to the sector with two wavenumbers of each sign, which contains no non-trivial resonance, so the cancellation follows without calculation. In complex normal variables the symmetry is the vanishing of the reduced Zakharov kernel whenever the product of the four wavenumbers is non-positive, and the known closed form of that kernel follows directly. The symmetry is the fourth-order instance of a selection rule valid at every order in these variables: no term of the Hamiltonian has a single wavenumber of the minority sign. The rule rests on the holomorphic structure of planar deep-water flow and on its square-root dispersion relation.
item.dc:creator: P\"aivo Simson

item.title: Development and control of G\"ortler vortices in the SD-2 serpentine diffuser
item.description: arXiv:2611.27298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates and controls the flow through a serpentine diffuser using wall-modeled large-eddy simulations (WMLES), with emphasis on the formation of streamwise vortices, their contribution to flow distortion, and their suppression using opposition control. Following Agrawal et al., AIAA Journal (2026), simulations are performed at three Mach numbers, $Ma_{AIP} =0.36, 0.46,0.54$. Adverse pressure gradients and centrifugal forces induced by geometric features of the diffuser promote flow separation and lead to the formation of counter-rotating G\"ortler vortices. Downstream of the second bend, the transition from an elliptical to a circular cross-section drives these vortices toward the centerline along the spanwise direction, ejecting low-momentum fluid from the near-wall region into the core. A steady opposition-control strategy using wall-normal velocity forcing is employed to attenuate the streamwise vortices. The control strategy increases pressure recovery, reduces flow distortion, and substantially suppresses total-pressure fluctuations across all three Mach numbers. The maximum flow distortion is reduced by $\approx 50\%$ at the two lower Mach numbers and by $34\%$ at $Ma_{AIP}=0.54$. The variance of the total-pressure fluctuations is reduced by approximately two orders of magnitude near the center of the AIP and by a factor of two near the periphery. An input-output power analysis further shows a net positive power gain at all three Mach numbers, with a maximum control efficiency of approximately $65\%$ at the lowest Mach number, although the power efficiency decreases significantly at higher Mach numbers due to the larger actuation amplitudes required.
item.dc:creator: Akhil Nekkanti, Rahul Agrawal, Sanjeeb Bose, Parviz Moin

item.title: How Meandering Flow Sculpts Ice
item.description: arXiv:2611.27358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ice-water phase change subject to a mean flow widely exists in the Cryosphere, with implications on glacier evolution, human transportation, flooding events, etc. Understanding the relevant phase change dynamics requires identifying the roles of shear and rotation due to the mean flow. Combining experiments, numerical simulations and theoretical modelling, we reveal the combined effects of shear and rotation on the coupled dynamics of water flow, heat transfer and phase change in an annular system. Increasing shear and rotation drive a stronger secondary circulation which significantly enhances global heat transfer and redistributes the radial heat flux, and eventually lead to a thinner equilibrium ice layer and a larger ice thickness difference in the radial direction. Further, we develop an integral thermal balance model that explains the mean ice thickness through estimating the additional heat transfer, and a local thermal balance model that explains the inner-outer ice thickness difference by relating it to the non-uniform convective heat flux. The local model shows qualitative agreement with field measurements when applied to an ice-covered meandering river. These results contribute to understanding the common physical mechanism for ice-water phase change under shear and rotation, offering a theoretical basis for explaining and predicting ice evolution in meandering rivers among other relevant scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Yihong Du, Jin Hu, Feng Wang, Lars ten Hacken, Ziqi Wang, Rui Yang, Enrico Calzavarini, Federico Toschi, Chao Sun

item.title: Regular reflection of shock waves: non-equilibrium effects for various steady flow parameters
item.description: arXiv:2611.27537v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A parametric study of the non-equilibrium region formed by the steady regular reflection of two symmetric oblique shock waves in a monatomic gas is performed using the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method. Three series of calculations are considered, with the incident-shock normal Mach number fixed at 2, 4 and 8, respectively. Within each series, the incidence angle is reduced while the normal strength of the incident shock remains unchanged. The decrease in angle primarily results in a longer non-equilibrium region of shock-wave interaction. Over the parameter range considered, the density-transition width along the plane of symmetry is approximately inversely proportional to the sine of the incidence angle. Increasing the normal Mach number enhances temperature anisotropy, the local temperature overshoot relative to the equilibrium downstream state, and the streamwise-velocity undershoot.
item.dc:creator: Yevgeniy Bondar, Maksim Timokhin

item.title: A sliding mode observer perspective on chaos synchronisation of turbulent flows
item.description: arXiv:2611.27568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State estimation of turbulent flows is challenging as infinitesimal prediction errors grow exponentially due to chaos. However, when signals from one chaotic system (the master) are injected into an identical system with different initial conditions (the slave), the slave can synchronise with the master --- a phenomenon observed in turbulent flows. From a control-theoretic perspective, this synchronisation problem can be viewed as observer design. We first show that synchronisation by direct substitution of observed variables into the slave system is equivalent to a sliding mode observer. This perspective enables the analytical verification of stability as well as the design of feedback for robustness. We focus on reduced-order Navier--Stokes models with quadratic non-linearities, a broad class of systems for which stability can be analysed by seeking Lyapunov functions through parameter-dependent linear matrix inequalities solved via semidefinite programming. Extending this framework, we develop a neural network approach combining a neural ordinary differential equation with a decoder to learn data-driven mappings from observation histories to companion forms, where observer design is greatly simplified. Results are demonstrated on the Lorenz system and a nine-dimensional reduced order model of a turbulent shear flow. This work opens opportunities in the rigorous development of observers for turbulent flows.
item.dc:creator: Defne E. Ozan, Andrew Wynn

item.title: A new restitution model for wet particle collisions using fully resolved numerical simulations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27593v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Particle collisions play a central role in wet particle processes such as granulation, drying, and chemical reactors, yet the influence of the liquid on the collision dynamics remains insufficiently understood. This study investigates the influence of liquid viscosity, liquid density, liquid content, impact velocity, solid density, and surface tension on the wet restitution coefficient using numerical simulations. In this study, a Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) framework is used that has been validated against dedicated experiments of wet-wet particle collisions, showing a good agreement for both liquid-bridge evolution and rebound dynamics. The restitution coefficient decreases with increasing liquid viscosity, liquid density, and liquid-to-solid density ratio, whereas increasing impact velocity increases rebound. The negligible influence of surface tension indicates that viscous dissipation is the dominant source of energy loss under the investigated conditions. As existing Stokes number formulations were found to only capture part of the governing physics, a generalized Stokes number is proposed to incorporate both the viscous and inertial response time scales. A modified restitution coefficient model based on the generalized Stokes number successfully collapses the numerical and experimental data onto a single trend and predicts the wet restitution coefficient with an RMSE of only 4.99%.
item.dc:creator: A. H. Huijgen, F. Bunke, S. Heinrich, Y. Tang, N. G. Deen, M. W. Baltussen

item.title: Impulsive ejection of Worthington jets by flow focusing. Influence of a soluble surfactant
item.description: arXiv:2611.27709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally investigate impulsive Worthington jet generation by flow focusing, considering the liquid meniscus location that maximizes the flow-focusing effect. This effect increases the jet velocity by up to two orders of magnitude over the bottom liquid velocity after impact. At sufficiently high liquid velocities, jet formation is governed primarily by inertia, making jet velocity largely independent of liquid viscosity, surface tension, and surfactant effects. Each liquid exhibits an optimum impact velocity that maximizes momentum transfer. Surfynol 465 lowers the impactvelocity threshold for water-jet emission and increases jet velocity by rapidly restoring equilibrium surface tension. In contrast, Triton X-100 has an almost negligible effect because of its slower adsorption kinetics. Importantly, both surfactants reduce jet diameter and, consequently, droplet size. This reduction is particularly significant with Surfynol 465 at high impact velocities, suggesting potential applications, for instance, in high-resolution printing technologies. The jet loaded with Surfynol 465 was even faster than that of the glycerine-water mixture with the same Ohnesorge and Weber numbers. This suggests that adding Surfynol 465 further accelerates jet emission, exceeding the speed attained by a clean interface with the same reduced equilibrium surface tension.
item.dc:creator: T. Gonz\'alez-Rubio, S. Rodr\'iguez-Aparicio, E. J. Vega, J. M. Montanero

item.title: Augmentation of cardiovascular flow measurements with generative diffusion models
item.description: arXiv:2611.27917v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cardiovascular imaging offers several ways to measure blood flow, but each provides an incomplete, resolution-limited, or noisy view of the underlying dynamics. Reconstructing the missing information is inherently ambiguous because several flow fields may be compatible with the same observation. Here, we investigate generative diffusion models as tools for cardiovascular-flow generation and reconstruction using a fully controlled state-of-the-art dataset from a digital twin of a healthy human left heart. First, we show how unconditional samples reproduce the changing anatomy and the highly fluctuating statistical properties of the flow throughout the cardiac cycle. Second, we test the conditional inference of our generative model by reconstructing an entire 2D planar section of geometry and flow configurations from a limited portion. Repeated reconstructions allow us to represent a range of plausible completions, going beyond a single deterministic estimate, while their mean retains the principal features of the reference flow. Comparison with a Gaussian process regression baseline on the same reduced domain highlights the main advantage of diffusion models: their reconstructed ensembles capture a broader range of velocity and gradient fluctuations, better encompassing ground-truth features that the baseline distributions can miss. Our results provide a quantitative proof of concept for probabilistic reconstruction of incomplete cardiovascular-flow measurements and demonstrate the potential for groundbreaking applications to the augmentation of in-vivo cardiovascular imaging data.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Guglietta, Tianyi Li, Francesco Viola, Luca Biferale

item.title: Effects of sinusoidal pitch amplitude and phase on power extraction and pitching-energy exchange in a single-blade vertical-axis turbine model
item.description: arXiv:2611.27941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sinusoidal blade pitching can improve vertical-axis turbine performance, but whether a blade could follow the same motion passively depends on the energy exchanged through pitching. This study experimentally examines 480 prescribed-pitch conditions using a single-blade model following a circular trajectory in a water channel at four tip-speed ratios (TSRs) from 1.25 to 3.14. The amplitude associated with the highest measured power decreases from 16{\deg} to 12{\deg} and then 8{\deg} as TSR increases, with the corresponding phase shifting from 0 to pi/4. At TSRs of 1.25 and 3.14, the cycle-averaged power coefficient increases from 0.0047 to 0.1037 and from 0.4698 to 0.5948, respectively. Pitching-energy maps show nearly neutral net hydrodynamic pitching work for the highest-performing motions at the two lower TSRs and net energy transfer from the flow to pitching at the two higher TSRs. Virtual damping narrows the positive-energy region, although the higher-TSR best-tested motions retain an energy surplus at nonzero damping. However, net energy transfer from the flow to pitching also occurs for motions with substantial power losses. At the lowest TSR, phase-resolved force measurements and particle image velocimetry link the gain to delayed dynamic-stall-vortex formation and shedding, prolonged favorable loading, and reduced subsequent negative power. At the highest TSR, the flow and loading change locally, with little alteration of the main power-producing event. The joint maps identify performance-enhancing motions with an energetic margin against assumed dissipation, providing candidates for further passive or assisted pitching studies.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Zhang, Anchi Li, Qimin Feng, Yuanhang Zhu, Qiang Zhong

item.title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.27351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cardiovascular fluid dynamics modeling relies heavily on mesh-based numerical methods such as Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). While accurate, these methods entail significant computational costs and complex meshing workflows that limit their translation to clinical practice. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless alternative that embeds the governing equations directly into neural network training. In this work, we propose a PINN framework for pulsatile blood flow in patient-specific geometries with dynamic lumped-parameter Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions representing distal vascular impedance. Coupling the Windkessel ODE to a 3D network raises two difficulties: the ODE alone does not fix the pressure level, and the local pressure variations that drive the flow are orders of magnitude smaller than the basal pressure imposed by the outlet. We address them by decomposing pressure into a time-dependent basal part and a spatially varying part, an initial condition and gauge for the Windkessel equation, a global mass-balance constraint, and a periodic Fourier embedding of time. Validated on 2D canonical channels (steady and pulsatile, with and without RCR outlet), the framework is then applied to a patient-specific right pulmonary artery, reproducing outlet flow, mean pressure, and the velocity and dynamic pressure fields with errors on the order of the data resolution. Finally, we solve the inverse problem of identifying the three Windkessel parameters of the outlet from synthetic data, recovering them with errors of about 0.3% from deliberately wrong initial values. Residual biases in the local pressure field and the need to test robustness to noisy clinical data remain open, but the results support PINNs as complementary tools for meshless hemodynamics and patient-specific digital twins.
item.dc:creator: Celia Taboada, Luis Nu\~nez, Ang\'elica Casero, Pedro Navas

item.title: Lacrymaria-like dynamics: compression and length change in active slender bodies
item.description: arXiv:2611.27577v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Length change is central to the behaviour of many active slender bodies, yet most elastohydrodynamic models of microscopic locomotion treat filaments as effectively inextensible. Here we introduce a compressible $N$-link formulation for planar active filaments, in which both bending angles and segment lengths are dynamical variables coupled through local hydrodynamic drag, modelled using resistive force theory. We first use the model to test whether passive extensibility can improve bending-driven swimming and crawling. Across the parameter ranges studied, passive compressibility usually reduces locomotion speed, indicating that axial compliance alone is not a robust mechanism for propulsion enhancement. We then prescribe active rest-length waves and show that compression can either enhance, suppress, or redirect locomotion depending on its phase, wavelength, and frequency relative to bending. Finally, motivated by the extensible neck dynamics of \textit{Lacrymaria olor}, we apply the method to clamped and free filaments driven by oscillatory follower forces. These examples show that elastic compression-bending coupling can reorganise swimming, exploration, and locomotion in strongly deforming active filaments.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'ement Moreau, Yukinori Nishigami, Johann H\'erault, Kenta Ishimoto

item.title: Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27670v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Suppressing vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder is a classical problem in active flow control.Model-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) learns such policies by interacting with the flow without differentiating its dynamics, which typically requires a large interaction budget. This study optimises closed-loop policies by differentiable simulation: control-loss gradients propagate through the simulated flow to the policy parameters, which are updated by reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The policy maps local velocity measurements to a jet amplitude imposed through differentiable synthetic-jet boundary conditions. In a two-dimensional confined cylinder wake at Rey=100, eight policy updates (about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation) give approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations, the drag level being comparable to reported DRL results. Suppression is sustained by feedback: a mean-matched constant jet does not maintain it, whereas the same policy responds similarly at three activation phases and recovers after upstream disturbances. A velocity-deviation reward alone retains strong suppression, and observations of two instantaneous velocity components at one near-wake or surface location reach about 99.8% suppression, whereas a single surface pressure leaves residual oscillations. Together with related DRL results, this suggests that reward and observation requirements here are set by policy optimisation and flow physics.
item.dc:creator: Siwen Zhang, Xizeng Zhao, Zhouteng Ye, Yulin Xie, Zesheng Yao

item.title: Combined effects of evaporation, sedimentation and solute crystallization on the dynamics of aerosol size distributions on multiple length and time scales
item.description: arXiv:2601.05876v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate three aspects of aerosol-mediated air-borne viral infection mechanisms on different length and time scales. First, we address the evolution of the size distribution of a non-interacting ensemble of droplets that are subject to evaporation and sedimentation using a sharp droplet-air interface model. From the exact solution of the evolution equation we derive the viral load in the air and show that it depends sensitively on the relative humidity. Secondly, from Molecular Dynamics simulations we extract the molecular reflection coefficient of single water molecules from the air-water interface. This parameter determines the water condensation and evaporation rate at a liquid droplet surface and therefore the evaporation rate of aqueous droplets. We find the reflection of water to be negligible at room temperature but to rise significantly at elevated temperatures and for grazing incidence angles. Thirdly, we derive a thermodynamically consistent three-dimensional diffuse-interface model for solute-containing droplets that is formulated as a three-phase Cahn-Hilliard/Allen-Cahn system. By numerically solving the coupled system of equations, we explore representative scenarios that show that this model reproduces and generalizes features of the sharp-interface model. These interconnected studies on the dynamics of aerosol droplet evaporation are relevant in order to quantitatively assess the airborne infection risk under varying environmental conditions.
item.dc:creator: Sina Zendehroud, Ole Kleinjung, Philip Loche, Lyd\'eric Bocquet, Roland R. Netz, Erica Ipocoana, Dirk Peschka, Marita Thomas

item.title: Two-way coupling in active suspensions suppresses mobility-selective accumulation and induces non-monotonic flow stabilization
item.description: arXiv:2607.02745v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Swimmers live in moving fluids: the flow organizes their spatial distribution, and their collective motion reshapes the flow in turn. We experimentally study the two-way coupling between a swarm of centimeter-scale swimmers (Artemia salina) and an electromagnetically driven quasi-two-dimensional cellular flow. We report two key findings, one in each direction of the coupling. First, at low swimmer density, the swarm recovers the mobility-selective accumulation onto the attracting hyperbolic Lagrangian coherent structures (LCSs) predicted by one-way-coupled simulations: the accumulation is strongest when the swimming speed is comparable to the flow speed. As the density increases, the swarm still accumulates on the LCSs, but the mobility selectivity is progressively lost. Second, we examine the back-action of the swarm on the LCSs. A swarm has previously been found to disrupt the LCSs. We find that the response depends on the swimmer density and the background forcing. Denser swarms tend to disrupt the LCSs more strongly, as previously reported. However, at stronger forcing, adding a moderate number of swimmers instead stabilizes the LCSs.
item.dc:creator: Ziyue Yu, Aineo M. Wu, Lei Fang

item.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part I: The gravity force term
item.description: arXiv:2611.24841v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The OpenFOAM solver interFoam for incompressible two-phase flows combines the single-phase PISO/PIMPLE algorithm for the pressure-velocity coupling with an interface advection step. It relies on the standard finite volume discretisation of the momentum equation, which assumes smooth fields, but across a water-air interface the density jumps by a factor of about 1000. The geometric Volume-of-Fluid method isoAdvector, used in interIsoFoam, made the advection step consistent with a sharp interface, but spurious velocities near it remain due to the momentum discretisation. This series revisits it term by term. Here we treat the gravity term, which acts only at the interface and depends on the local interface height. Both solvers crudely assign this height using the face centre positions. We show that this is a key source of the spurious air velocities. Taking the height from the reconstructed interface instead gives an exact discrete balance between pressure and gravity for a horizontal interface on any mesh. We implement this geometric gravity model in a new solver, interIsoGoam. In a tilted box of still water, where the original solvers give air speeds of metres per second, it keeps the velocity of order $10^{-9}$ m/s. This holds for density ratios up to $10^7$ and, with a hydrostatic initial pressure, on skewed and locally refined meshes. In a progressive wave, interIsoGoam has the lowest maximum velocity of the three solvers. At maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below it therefore needs up to 43 % fewer steps and up to 38 % less wall-clock time. At 0.5 the wave grows by up to 12 % over 15 periods, so we recommend 0.1 or less. One error remains, namely an overprediction of the horizontal water velocity below the wave crest. All three solvers exhibit this error, which grows steadily with time. In Part II we trace this error to the implicit discretisation of the momentum convection term.
item.dc:creator: Johan Roenby, Konstantinos Missios, Kasper M{\o}ller, Sithik Aliyar, Henning Scheufler

item.title: Consistent interfacial flow numerics - Part II: The momentum convection term
item.description: arXiv:2611.24866v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The two-phase Volume-of-Fluid solvers of OpenFOAM overpredict the horizontal water velocity near the crest of a water wave, and the error grows as the wave propagates. Part I of this series removed the spurious air velocities caused by the gravity term but left this error unchanged. Here we show that it is caused by the momentum convection term. Its mass flux is computed in the interface advection step from the velocity at the start of the time step, whereas the convected velocity is taken at the end of the step, because convection is discretised implicitly. In a progressive wave, where the horizontal and vertical velocities are 90 degrees out of phase, this time lag produces an upward flux of horizontal momentum, proportional to the time step, which accumulates in a spurious current near the surface. The same mismatch makes the response to a force depend on the density at the wrong time level. Explicit convection removes the lag and makes the response consistent with the gravity force, but requires the convected face velocity at the interface to be taken from the upwind cell. Only then is the new velocity of a cell a weighted average of old velocities, whatever the density ratio. We demonstrate both requirements with prescribed flows and with the full solver. For a progressive wave, explicit convection with upwind face velocities at the interface reduces the overprediction of the crest velocity from 26-31 % to within 1 % and removes the near-surface current. The resulting solver, fluxinator, is meant for maximum Courant numbers of 0.1 and below, where it keeps the wave height within 1.5 % over 15 periods on meshes with six or more cells per wave height. Because the spurious velocities that limit the time step are removed, it needs 34-42 % less wall-clock time than interFoam for the tested wave.
item.dc:creator: Johan Roenby

item.title: The Well: a Large-Scale Collection of Diverse Physics Simulations for Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2412.00568v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning based surrogate models offer researchers powerful tools for accelerating simulation-based workflows. However, as standard datasets in this space often cover small classes of physical behavior, it can be difficult to evaluate the efficacy of new approaches. To address this gap, we introduce the Well: a large-scale collection of datasets containing numerical simulations of a wide variety of spatiotemporal physical systems. The Well draws from domain experts and numerical software developers to provide 15TB of data across 16 datasets covering diverse domains such as biological systems, fluid dynamics, acoustic scattering, as well as magneto-hydrodynamic simulations of extra-galactic fluids or supernova explosions. These datasets can be used individually or as part of a broader benchmark suite. To facilitate usage of the Well, we provide a unified PyTorch interface for training and evaluating models. We demonstrate the function of this library by introducing example baselines that highlight the new challenges posed by the complex dynamics of the Well. The code and data is available at https://github.com/PolymathicAI/the_well.
item.dc:creator: Ruben Ohana, Michael McCabe, Lucas Meyer, Rudy Morel, Fruzsina J. Agocs, Miguel Beneitez, Marsha Berger, Blakesley Burkhart, Keaton Burns, Stuart B. Dalziel, Drummond B. item.title: Inpainting physics: self-supervised learning for context-driven fluid simulation
item.description: arXiv:2605.08832v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural surrogate models for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are typically trained as forward operators that map explicit problem specifications, such as geometry and boundary conditions, to solution fields. This ties the model to the conditioning variables seen during training and limits reuse under boundary-condition shifts or local geometry changes. We propose to reformulate steady CFD inference as an inpainting problem: instead of training on explicit boundary conditions, we learn a self-supervised prior over velocity fields and impose boundary constraints only during inference by fixing known regions such as inlet, outlet or unchanged regions from previous simulations. To scale this idea to large 3D meshes, we introduce a local neighbourhood tokeniser that represents high-resolution velocity fields as compact spatial latent tokens and train latent flow-matching and masked-autoencoder models on these tokens. On simulations of intracranial aneurysm flow, our method reconstructs full velocity fields from sparse boundary context, outperforms supervised neural surrogates under boundary-condition and dataset shift and enables local geometry editing by reusing unchanged simulation context. These results suggest that viewing CFD inference as context-conditioned inpainting can turn neural surrogates from task-specific predictors into reusable flow priors. Code and demo are available at https://inpainting-physics.com.
item.dc:creator: Jonas Weidner, Yeray Martin-Ruisanchez, Daniel Rueckert, Benedikt Wiestler, Julian Suk

item.title: Energy spectra and cascade in the spin turbulence of a driven spinor Bose-Einstein condensate
item.description: arXiv:2606.00766v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the spin-interaction energy spectrum of spin turbulence in a driven spinor Bose-Einstein condensate. Continuous spin driving of a spin-1 condensate produces a nonequilibrium steady state with spatially fluctuating magnetization. We observe a power-law scaling consistent with the $-7/3$ exponent predicted for spin-wave turbulence, which persists across our full range of drive strengths despite substantial changes in the spectral anisotropy. After switching off the drive, we track the free-decay evolution and find evidence consistent with a direct cascade of spin-interaction energy toward higher wavenumbers. These results establish an energy-spectral hallmark of spin turbulence and enable quantitative studies of cascade dynamics in spinor superfluids.
item.dc:creator: Junghoon Lee, Jongmin Kim, Donggyu Lee, Yong-il Shin
